claim: Word-level semantic priming is a real effect, but pure-meaning priming without association is small (d about .26) and associative priming about twice as large (d about .51).
agent_test: Compare retrieval of meaning-only neighbours vs associated neighbours at equal tokens; expect meaning-only gain about half.
audit_note: d=.26 vs .51 comes only from Lucas (2000), which is listed twice (a11 and b01 are the same paper); Hutchison (2003) is a critique of Lucas that reports no d values, so the numeric claim rests on a single meta-analysis (numbers themselves match).

claim: Real priming effects shrink in large varied samples: first-associate priming was 26/20 ms in the Semantic Priming Project versus 42/60 ms in an earlier regression study; expect demos to overstate gains.
agent_test: Report held-out gains of graph spread on a fresh item set, not on the tuning set.

claim: Multi-link (mediated) spread is weak: de Groot found no mediated priming in standard lexical decision across 7 experiments; later work finds small effects (about 8-32 ms) only when strategy is blocked.
agent_test: Sweep hop depth 1..4; expect the largest gain from hop 1 to 2 and flat or negative beyond 3.

claim: Priming has an automatic fast part and a strategic slow part, but no universal SOA separates them.
agent_test: Run a cheap code-only expansion first and a model-guided search only when a signal fires; compare with always-on search.
audit_note: Hutchison is author of both sources (Heyman paper is KU Leuven-led), so independence is partial; both do support the claim and the 'no universal SOA' point is explicit in Hutchison 2003.

claim: Association and feature overlap both contribute to priming; category coordinates alone do not prime automatically. Keep both association edges and similarity edges.
agent_test: Ablate edge types (co-occurrence vs embedding similarity) in the memory graph.

claim: Associative rank can matter more than raw link strength; other-associate priming can be absent or negative.
agent_test: Compare thresholding by weight with taking top-k by rank.

claim: Personalized PageRank over an LLM-built KG beats dense retrieval on entity-heavy multi-hop sets (2Wiki R@5 89.1 vs 68.2) but not on HotpotQA (77.7 vs 79.3) or much on MuSiQue (51.9 vs 49.2). Independent test (Han et al.) shows the multi-hop margin over dense is only about 3 points (HotpotQA F1 63.01 vs 60.04; MultiHop-RAG 70.27 vs 67.02).
agent_test: Run graph spread vs dense retrieval on our own item mix; split by single-hop and multi-hop.

claim: Graph spread is not uniformly better: independent test found plain RAG wins single-hop (NQ F1 64.78 vs HippoRAG2 61.03) and naive triple-only KG retrieval loses badly (34.28).
agent_test: Gate graph spread on question type; compare with plain retrieval at equal tokens.

claim: The spreading step itself carries the gain: adding direct neighbours without PPR is worse than seeds alone (avg R@5 58.4 vs 72.9 full; seeds only 56.2).
agent_test: Ablate multi-hop weighted spread against one-hop neighbour stuffing.

claim: Spreading activation finds complete evidence sets that similarity search misses: all-recall AR@5 2Wiki 75.7 vs 37.1, average 52.0 vs 37.4.
agent_test: Measure all-evidence-found rate, not only recall.

claim: Unconstrained spreading converges to a near query-independent state; hop limits, fan-out limits, decay below one and thresholds are required. Gating each hop by query similarity improved F1 +3.6 to +7.4 and cut latency 1.5-4.9x.
agent_test: Compare uniform spread with query-gated spread at equal tokens.
audit_note: First half (convergence to near query-independent state) rests on a secondhand literature review in SA-RAG citing earlier work; the gating numbers come from a single paper (Glybovets and Makarov) listed twice.

claim: Depth matters more than decay: going from 1 to 2 hops adds 18.8 F1 (2Wiki) and 12.7 (MuSiQue); beyond 3 hops gains vanish; decay sweep 0.3-1.0 changes F1 by under 4.
agent_test: Fix depth 2-3; do not spend effort tuning decay.
audit_note: Minor slip: decay sweep changes F1 by 2.8 (2Wiki) and 4.0 (MuSiQue), not strictly under 4, and the paper says it lies within the CI; depth gain from the Glybovets paper only (n=500), 'beyond 3' backed by SA-RAG.

claim: Hub damping (fan effect) is needed: removing it drops SYNAPSE average F1 from 40.5 to 36.1 and open-domain F1 from 25.9 to 16.8.
agent_test: Ablate degree normalisation in the memory graph walk.

claim: Temporal decay in agent memory matters for time questions: removing node decay cut SYNAPSE temporal F1 from 50.1 to 14.2.
agent_test: Ablate recency decay on time-dependent questions.

claim: Graph memory holds up when the query shares few words with the evidence: SYNAPSE dropped 5.3-7.4% on low-similarity subsets versus 43-56% for A-Mem.
agent_test: Build a low-lexical-overlap test slice and compare dense vs graph retrieval.

claim: Graph spread plus iterative retrieval is complementary: SA-RAG+CoT reached 75 (MuSiQue) and 87 (2Wiki) correctness vs 46/48 naive, with small samples (100 questions).
agent_test: Combine code-run spread with an iterative model query loop; compare each alone at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match the SA-RAG paper (phi4 reader; listed three times, one paper); Han et al. only qualitatively agrees that iterative retrieval helps graph methods on multi-hop.

claim: Agent memory with spreading activation beat other memory systems on LoCoMo (F1 40.5 vs Zep 39.7, A-Mem 33.3) with about 95% fewer tokens than full context; HeLa-Mem reports spreading ablation 34.74 vs 32.19. Caveat: no isolated independent re-test of SYNAPSE exists; a SYNAPSE-style re-implementation (SuperLocalMemory V3.3) gained on multi-hop but lost 14.9 points on single-hop vs its earlier version, and HeLa-Mem's spread ablation is only -2.6 F1.
agent_test: Run a spreading-activation memory against flat vector memory on long-history tasks at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs reproduce some priming only weakly or conditionally: GPT-4o mini priming vanishes under multiple imputation (p=.088); GPT-3 shows priming only in some prompt formats; BERT priming fades under strong context.
agent_test: Do not assume the model's internal associations spread like human ones; test if memory expansion is needed.

claim: LLM-generated association networks reproduce human spreading-activation priming predictions (effect sizes 0.859-0.869 vs 0.870 human; rho about -0.61 vs -0.63) and LLM shortest paths predict human RT.
agent_test: Use an LLM to seed association edges when no corpus graph exists; validate against held-out pairs.
audit_note: Minor: effect sizes 0.859/0.869 omit Claude Haiku (0.866, in range) and rho -0.61 omits Haiku at -0.662 (stronger than human -0.626); only 50 prime-target pairs.

claim: Embedding-driven spreading in ACT-R only slightly beats frequency plus length baselines for item-level RT (rho 0.50 vs 0.48).
agent_test: Treat embedding similarity as nearly as good as hand-built association links.

claim: Pure semantic vs associative structure layers do not carry over to LLMs: human bias falls from associative to categorical layers, but Mistral and Llama3 show no consistent pattern.
agent_test: Audit spread-based retrieval for stereotyped associations.

claim: The 2012 replication failures concerned behavioural (social) priming; semantic priming is described as well established (Meyer 2014, via Wikipedia) and has a large dataset in the Semantic Priming Project (1,661 targets, 768 subjects, 4 universities), so those failures are not known to extend to word-level semantic priming.
agent_test: Tag evidence by priming type.
audit_note: Neither source says social-priming replication failures 'do not apply'; Wikipedia only reports that the 2012 failures concerned behavioural priming and cites Meyer 2014 (a short letter) saying semantic priming is well established, and the Semantic Priming Project (Hutchison et al. 2013) only shows a large dataset exists, not that it is immune or independently replicated.
claim_before_audit: Social priming failures from the replication crisis do not apply to word-level semantic priming, which has large datasets.

claim: Seed by matching the whole query to stored fact-triples (or passages), not by extracting entities or matching to bare nodes: in HippoRAG 2, passage recall@5 averaged 87.1 (query-to-triple) vs 74.6 (NER-to-node) vs 59.6 (query-to-node); dropping passage nodes gave 81.0. Note: the critique's gap 7 pair 87.1 vs 74.6 was mislabelled.
agent_test: Run seed-by-triple, seed-by-entity, seed-by-node on our own memory; expect triple/passage seeds best.

claim: A cheap router can decide when to spread: a small MLP on query syntax raised mixed-benchmark accuracy from 65.1 (dense) to 71.6, at 2.19 s vs 3.23 s per query for always-graph; prompted fact-vs-reasoning classification and simply concatenating both contexts also beat either alone. Dense RAG wins single-hop lookup (NQ F1 64.78 vs 61.03 for HippoRAG 2).
agent_test: Rule: spread only when the thought names 2+ entities or asks a relation; compare to always-spread on a mixed set.

claim: Graph-RAG variants built on LLM-extracted relations alone are weak: triples-only graphs scored NQ F1 34.28 and HotpotQA 25.02 vs dense 64.78 / 60.04; adding source text recovered part (50.27 / 42.60). Only about 65% of answer entities appear in the extracted graph.
agent_test: Keep edges as routes to raw text; log how many gold entities are in the graph.

claim: Three edge types have evidence in agent memory: LLM-extracted relation plus synonym plus passage-context edges (HippoRAG 2), usage-learned co-activation edges (HeLa-Mem, spread ablation -2.6 F1 on LoCoMo), and embedding-similarity links (SYNAPSE). No study compares them on equal footing.
agent_test: Head-to-head ablation of three edge types at equal tokens on our tasks.

claim: HippoRAG 2's lead over dense retrieval held while the corpus grew 4x (NQ and MuSiQue segments), but multi-hop accuracy still fell at a similar rate for both. Largest graphs tested were about 314k nodes and 2.7M edges; nothing was found at millions of nodes.
agent_test: Track accuracy against memory size; add pruning before nodes pass the tested scale.

claim: Token cost of graph retrieval varies by 3 orders of magnitude: dense 879, HippoRAG 2 1,008, RAPTOR 3,441, MS-GraphRAG local 38,707, global 331,375 prompt tokens (novel corpus). Passage-linked PPR is the near-equal-token option.
agent_test: Report accuracy per prompt token, not accuracy alone.

claim: Stopping rules: a learned Q-network stop beats fixed depth by 1-3 F1 on two of three multi-hop sets and a prompted stop check adds nothing; a training-free evidence-coverage stop (HALT) avoids searching on 17-45% of loops without losing EM, and agents often run to budget (78-88% of questions for a 3B agent) yet also under-search. Fixed T=3 stays a sound default.
agent_test: Compare fixed T=3 to a coverage-based stop on our multi-hop set.

claim: Association graphs built by LLM carry stereotypes and are narrower than human ones (unique responses: humans 116,640, Llama3 105,367, Mistral 41,369, Haiku 15,275). A spreading-activation audit (prime demographic words, compare final activation of stereotype-consistent vs inconsistent targets) works on such graphs, but no study has shown that this shifts retrieval outputs.
agent_test: Run the prime-and-spread audit on our memory graph before and after a retrieval policy change.

claim: No source compares graph spread against dense retrieval plus an LLM query rewrite at equal tokens. The nearest items are an embedding-level iterative rewriter (TreeHop, 92.8-97.8% lower latency than LLM rewriting) and iterative RAG (IRCoT) reinforcing both RAG and GraphRAG gains.
agent_test: Build the missing test: dense, dense+rewrite, spread, spread+rewrite at equal tokens, split single vs multi-hop.
